title: Animism
summary: The belief, found in most traditional cultures, that living things and sometimes places are inhabited by spirits. It is often treated as the oldest form of religion.

title: Greek gods as archetypes
summary: The Olympian gods each personify a domain of human character: war, love, cunning, craft. They quarrel, scheme and take sides in human affairs, as in Homer.

title: Genesis and the Hebrew Bible
summary: The opening chapter of the Bible, in which God separates light from darkness and the waters above from those below, then makes plants, animals and humans. It is usually read as an account of the creation of the physical world in six days.

title: Pythagoras
summary: Greek thinker whose school held that number is the basis of reality. Later tradition says the school was thrown into scandal by the discovery of irrational quantities.

title: Logos
summary: Greek for word, reason or rational order: the principle by which the cosmos is intelligible. The Gospel of John opens with it ('In the beginning was the Word'), carrying the idea into Christianity.

title: Buddhism and meditation
summary: A contemplative tradition that studies experience from the inside through meditation, teaching that the self is constructed and that suffering comes from attachment. Advanced practitioners report being able to deconstruct ordinary perception and selfhood.

title: Plato: forms and the cave
summary: Plato held that behind the changing things we perceive there are ideal, timeless forms (the perfect triangle, the ideal table). In mathematics, 'Platonism' is the view that mathematical objects really exist independently of minds.

title: Aristotle
summary: Greek philosopher who systematised logic, physics and psychology. He described the soul (psyche) not as a ghostly substance but as the organising form of a living body, with vegetative, animal and rational layers.

title: Stoicism
summary: A school of philosophy teaching that we suffer from our judgments about events rather than the events themselves, and that we should concern ourselves only with what is in our control.

title: Christianity
summary: The religion built on the life and teaching of Jesus; for most of European history the Church was its unifying institution. Beyond its beliefs, it was an organisation that coordinated millions of people for centuries.

title: Thomas Aquinas
summary: Medieval theologian who merged Aristotle with Christian doctrine. He argued for God as the necessary ground of existence and described seven virtues: four practical ones (temperance, justice, prudence, courage) and three theological ones (faith, hope, love).

title: The golem
summary: A clay figure brought to life by a rabbi to serve and protect, which follows instructions literally and can run out of control. The best-known version, first written down in the nineteenth century, is about the sixteenth-century Rabbi Loew of Prague.

title: René Descartes
summary: French philosopher famous for 'I think, therefore I am' and for dividing reality into extended stuff (res extensa) and thinking stuff (res cogitans), the classic statement of mind-body dualism.

title: Occasionalism
summary: A post-Cartesian doctrine that mind and body never directly interact; God causes the matching events on each side on every occasion.

title: Empiricism: Locke and Hume
summary: A long dispute about the source of knowledge: experience of the world (empiricists such as Locke and Hume) or reasoning from first principles (rationalists such as Descartes and Leibniz).

title: Idealism
summary: The view that reality is fundamentally mental and the physical world is an appearance within mind. Bernardo Kastrup's 'analytic idealism' is a current version.

title: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
summary: German polymath who co-invented calculus and dreamed of a universal symbolic language in which disputes could be settled by calculation ('let us calculate').

title: La Mettrie: Man a Machine
summary: A scandalous Enlightenment pamphlet arguing that humans are entirely physical machines, not different in kind from animals, and that mind is a function of organised matter.

title: The Enlightenment
summary: The 18th-century European movement that put reason, evidence and individual autonomy above religious and traditional authority.

title: Immanuel Kant
summary: German philosopher who tried to ground morality in reason alone: act only on rules you could will to be universal laws, regardless of culture or consequences.

title: Utilitarianism
summary: The ethical theory that the right action is the one producing the greatest total wellbeing, in principle a calculus over pleasures and pains. It was developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill and underlies much of effective altruism.

title: G. W. F. Hegel
summary: German idealist who saw history as the process by which Spirit (Geist) comes to know itself. Progress, for him, happens through contradictions that are overcome at a higher level.

title: Cell theory
summary: The discovery that all living things are made of cells and that the cell is the basic unit of life.

title: Charles Darwin
summary: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection explained the design of living things without a designer.

title: Du Bois-Reymond: Ignorabimus
summary: The physiologist du Bois-Reymond declared that science will never know what matter and force are, or how matter gives rise to consciousness: 'ignorabimus', we shall never know.

title: Cantor's set theory
summary: Cantor showed that infinite sets come in different sizes: the set of all subsets of a set is always larger than the set itself. Applied to 'the set of all sets' this produces contradictions.

title: Epiphenomenalism
summary: The view that conscious experience is a by-product of brain activity with no causal influence on the physical world, like the steam-whistle of a locomotive.

title: Franz Brentano
summary: German-born philosopher-psychologist who taught in Vienna and revived the idea of intentionality: mental states are always 'about' something. He taught Husserl and Freud.

title: Emergence
summary: The idea that wholes can have properties their parts lack, as wetness belongs to water but not to a single molecule. The disputed question is whether emergent properties are merely convenient descriptions or genuinely new causes.

title: Early experimental psychology
summary: In the 19th century Wilhelm Wundt, Gustav Fechner and Hermann von Helmholtz turned the study of mind into a laboratory science, measuring sensation, attention and reaction and proposing theories of emotion and will.

title: Gottlob Frege
summary: German logician who invented modern predicate logic and tried to derive arithmetic from pure logic. Russell found a paradox in his system, which set off the crisis in the foundations of mathematics.

title: Peano axioms
summary: A handful of axioms that define the natural numbers and arithmetic: there is a zero, every number has a successor, and induction holds.

title: William James: The Principles of Psychology
summary: The founding textbook of American psychology, known for its descriptions of the stream of consciousness, attention and the self.

title: Constructive mathematics and intuitionism
summary: A school of mathematics that accepts an object only if you can give a procedure to construct it, rejecting proofs that merely assert existence and treating infinity as a never-finished process.

title: Russell and Whitehead
summary: Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Does it contain itself? If it does, it doesn't; if it doesn't, it does. The paradox showed that naive set theory is inconsistent.

title: Phenomenology
summary: Husserl proposed studying experience exactly as it is given. Each act of consciousness (noesis) is directed at an object as it is meant (noema), and philosophy should 'bracket' the taken-for-granted existence of the outside world (epoché) to describe how things appear.

title: Hilbert's programme
summary: Hilbert asked mathematicians to put all of mathematics into one formal axiom system and to prove, using only simple finite reasoning, that the system is consistent; he expected it also to be complete, so that every true statement could be derived.

title: Ludwig Wittgenstein
summary: Austrian philosopher. His early work tried to define exactly what can be said in a logical language; his later work argued that meaning comes from how language is used in life.

title: Freud and psychoanalysis
summary: Freud pictured the mind as three agencies: the id (drives), the ego (the self that negotiates with reality) and the superego (internalised rules). Psychoanalysis interprets behaviour as the outcome of their conflicts.

title: Qualia
summary: The 'what it is like' qualities of experience: the redness of red, the painfulness of pain. Many philosophers think they resist physical explanation.

title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
summary: Gödel proved that any consistent formal system rich enough to do arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. He did it by encoding statements about the system as numbers inside the system.

title: Alfred Tarski
summary: Polish logician who gave the standard formal definition of truth for logical languages and put semantics on a rigorous footing.

title: Alan Turing and computability
summary: English mathematician who defined computation with his abstract machine, helped found AI with the 1950 imitation-game paper, and late in life modelled how chemical patterns form in biology. During the Second World War he led the Bletchley Park section that broke German naval Enigma and designed the Bombe machine used to do it.
parts: Computing Machinery and Intelligence (the Turing test)

title: Lambda calculus and combinators
summary: Different formal definitions of what it means to compute (Turing's machines, Church's lambda calculus, Schönfinkel's combinators) turned out to be equivalent. The Church-Turing thesis says they capture everything that can be computed at all.

title: Behaviorism
summary: The school that restricted psychology to observable behaviour and treated talk of inner mental representations as unscientific. Skinner explained behaviour through its consequences: actions that are reinforced become more frequent.

title: Maslow: A Theory of Human Motivation
summary: Maslow's ranking of human needs, from bodily needs up to self-fulfilment.

title: McCulloch–Pitts neurons
summary: McCulloch and Pitts showed in 1943 that networks of simple threshold units can compute logical functions. In 1986 Rumelhart and McClelland's 'Parallel Distributed Processing' revived neural networks as models of cognition.

title: Schrödinger: life as negentropy
summary: In 'What is Life?' Schrödinger suggested that organisms stay ordered by feeding on 'negative entropy': they export disorder to their environment.

title: John von Neumann and the first computers
summary: Hungarian-American polymath who shaped game theory, quantum mechanics and the stored-program computer architecture that bears his name. He also designed self-reproducing automata, an early formal model of life.

title: Claude Shannon and information theory
summary: Shannon defined information as reduction of uncertainty, measurable in bits, and showed how much of it can be sent over a noisy channel.

title: Cybernetics
summary: The mid-century science of control and feedback in animals and machines, which grew out of control engineering and fed into systems theory and neural networks. Norbert Wiener named it in 1948; its core idea is that purposeful behaviour comes from feedback loops.

title: Materialism and physicalism
summary: The thesis that everything that exists is physical or depends on the physical, with no extra mental or supernatural ingredients. It is the default position in most of contemporary science and analytic philosophy.

title: Turing's morphogenesis
summary: Turing showed that interacting chemicals that diffuse at different rates spontaneously form spots and stripes. Neural cellular automata are a modern descendant: grids of identical cells that learn local rules to grow and repair a pattern.

title: Developmental stage theories
summary: Theories that describe mental growth as a series of stages: Piaget for children's thinking, Loevinger for ego development, Kohlberg for moral reasoning.

title: The Doors of Perception
summary: Huxley's report of taking mescaline, in which he suggests the brain normally filters a much wider field of awareness.

title: The founding of AI
summary: The 1956 summer meeting at Dartmouth College where the term 'artificial intelligence' was adopted and the field was founded on the bet that every aspect of intelligence can be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.

title: Cortical columns
summary: The neocortex appears to be built from repeating vertical circuits: minicolumns of about a hundred neurons, bundled into larger columns. Mountcastle proposed that these columns are the cortex's basic, general-purpose computing unit.

title: Many-worlds interpretation
summary: The reading of quantum mechanics in which the wave function never collapses; every possible outcome happens in a separate branch of the universe. Hugh Everett proposed it in 1957; observers split along with everything else, so each copy sees a single outcome.

title: Marvin Minsky
summary: Co-founder of the field of artificial intelligence at MIT. In 'The Society of Mind' (1986) and 'The Emotion Machine' (2006) he described the mind as a large crowd of simple cooperating processes, with no single principle behind it.

title: Noam Chomsky
summary: Linguist who argued that language rests on an innate grammar faculty, and a long-standing sceptic that statistical models tell us anything about the mind. His work in the 1950s helped end behaviourism and start cognitive science.

title: Pandemonium model
summary: An early model of perception as a crowd of 'demons', each shouting when it detects its pattern, with higher demons listening for the loudest.

title: Functionalism and computationalism
summary: Functionalism says a mental state is defined by what it does, not what it is made of. Computationalism adds that what minds do can be described as computation.

title: Stanisław Lem
summary: Polish science fiction writer and philosopher of technology. 'Solaris' (1961) is about an alien mind humans cannot understand; 'Golem XIV' (1981) is a set of lectures given by a superhuman computer to humanity.

title: Solomonoff induction
summary: Inventor of algorithmic probability, a mathematically ideal (though uncomputable) theory of learning by preferring the shortest programs that explain the data. He attended the 1956 Dartmouth workshop and his ideas underlie later formal theories of universal intelligence.

title: Alexey Ivakhnenko
summary: Soviet-Ukrainian mathematician who trained multi-layer networks in the 1960s (the Group Method of Data Handling), often cited as the earliest deep learning.

title: Symbolic AI
summary: The first paradigm of AI: represent knowledge as symbols and logical rules and reason over them. Expert systems encoded specialists' rules by hand.

title: ELIZA
summary: An early chat program that imitated a therapist using simple pattern matching. Many users felt understood by it.

title: Timothy Leary and the eight-circuit model
summary: A counter-culture model that describes eight 'circuits' of the nervous system, from basic survival up to mystical states.

title: Digital physics
summary: The hypothesis that the universe is, at bottom, a discrete computation such as a cellular automaton. Zuse proposed it in 'Rechnender Raum' (1969); Fredkin and Wolfram developed it.

title: Conway's Game of Life
summary: A grid of cells that live or die according to how many neighbours they have. From these few rules arise gliders, self-copying patterns and even complete computers.

title: Mirror test
summary: A test of self-recognition: put a mark on an animal's face and see whether it uses a mirror to investigate the mark on itself.

title: Holonomic brain theory
summary: Pribram's idea that the brain stores information like a hologram, spread across interference patterns, so each part contains something of the whole. It was inspired by the fact that memories survive quite large local brain damage.

title: Dreyfus: What Computers Still Can't Do
summary: A philosopher's long-running critique of symbolic AI. Dreyfus argued that human skill rests on bodily know-how and context that cannot be written down as explicit rules.

title: Gaia hypothesis
summary: The proposal that life on Earth, taken together, regulates the planet's atmosphere and climate as if it were a single organism. James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis proposed it in the 1970s.

title: Nagel: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
summary: Nagel argues that an organism is conscious if there is something it is like to be that organism, and that objective science seems to leave this point of view out.

title: The language of thought
summary: Claims that thinking happens in an inner symbolic code with a grammar, somewhat like a language. This is the classic statement of symbolic cognitive science.

title: Adaptive Resonance Theory
summary: Grossberg's theory that the brain learns stably by matching top-down expectations against bottom-up input; on his account every conscious state is such a 'resonance' between the two.

title: Dawkins: selfish genes and memes
summary: Dawkins reframed evolution as competition between genes, with organisms as the vehicles genes build to get themselves copied. The book also introduced the 'meme'.

title: Jaynes: the bicameral mind
summary: Jaynes claimed that until about 3,000 years ago people did not experience an inner self; they heard the commands of gods as voices, produced by one half of the brain and obeyed by the other.

title: Scripts, Plans, Goals and Understanding
summary: Proposed that people understand everyday situations through 'scripts', stored step-by-step outlines such as what happens in a restaurant.

title: Aaron Sloman
summary: British philosopher and AI researcher. He argued that philosophy of mind should be done by designing working minds, and he proposed the CogAff scheme that sorts mental processes into reactive, deliberative and reflective layers.

title: Hofstadter: strange loops
summary: In 'Gödel, Escher, Bach' and 'I Am a Strange Loop', Hofstadter suggests the self arises when a symbol system becomes able to refer to itself, a tangled feedback loop like Gödel's self-referential sentence. On this view 'I' is a pattern, not a thing, and could in principle exist in other substrates.

title: Lucid dreaming
summary: Dreaming while knowing that you are dreaming, sometimes with control over the dream. It has been confirmed in sleep laboratories, where dreamers signal with agreed eye movements.

title: Perceptual illusions
summary: If a face is shown upside down with the eyes and mouth flipped, it looks normal until you turn the picture upright, when it looks grotesque.

title: Searle: the Chinese room
summary: Berkeley philosopher who held that consciousness is a biological product of the brain's specific causal powers, like digestion, so that a program alone, however clever, cannot have it. His Chinese Room thought experiment is the best-known argument that manipulating symbols is not the same as understanding them.

title: The Mandelbrot set
summary: The Mandelbrot set is an infinitely detailed shape generated by repeating one tiny formula. It is a standard example of unlimited complexity from a simple rule.

title: The binding problem and neural synchrony
by: Anne Treisman & Garry Gelade; Peter Milner; Francis Crick & Christof Koch
summary: The question of how the brain joins separately processed features such as colour, shape and motion into one perceived object. Proposed answers include an attention-driven integration step and the synchronised firing of the neurons involved.

title: Kegan's stages of adult development
summary: Harvard psychologist's model in which adults can move from absorbing their beliefs from their group (stage 3), to reasoning independently (stage 4), to seeing how identities and value systems are themselves constructed (stage 5). Each stage makes an object of what the previous stage was unreflectively subject to.

title: Quantum computing
summary: Computers that use quantum superposition and entanglement to solve certain problems, such as factoring, far faster than any known classical method. Building them is hard because quantum states are destroyed by the slightest disturbance from the environment.

title: Two visual streams
summary: Visual processing in the cortex splits into a ventral 'what' pathway that identifies objects and a dorsal 'where/how' pathway that locates them and guides action.

title: Libet's readiness-potential experiments
summary: Experiments in which brain activity leading to a voluntary movement began a fraction of a second before people reported deciding to move.

title: The explanatory gap
summary: Levine's name for the gap between any physical or functional description of the brain and an explanation of why it feels the way it does.

title: Braitenberg: Vehicles
summary: A short book of thought experiments. Very simple wheeled machines with a few sensors and motors seem to show fear, love or curiosity, which suggests that complex-looking behaviour can come from simple wiring.

title: Cyc
summary: A decades-long project to hand-code millions of common-sense facts and rules so that a machine could reason like a person. Doug Lenat started it in 1984; it never produced general intelligence and became the emblem of hand-built AI.

title: Boltzmann machine
by: Geoffrey Hinton, Terrence Sejnowski, David Ackley
summary: A neural network in which units constrain each other and the whole settles into a low-energy state consistent with the inputs. The restricted version (RBM) drops within-layer links to make training feasible and helped launch deep learning.

title: Norbert Bischof
summary: German psychologist who modelled motivation, attachment and social distance as control systems.

title: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
summary: MIT's classic introductory programming textbook. It opens by describing computational processes as abstract beings that inhabit computers and are conjured by programs, like spirits by spells.

title: Autocatalytic networks and autopoiesis
by: Stuart Kauffman; Wim Hordijk & Mike Steel; Humberto Maturana & Francisco Varela
summary: Models of how a set of parts can come to produce and maintain itself as a whole, first used to explain the origin of life. Autopoiesis is the related idea of a system that continually makes its own components.

title: Connectionism and backpropagation
summary: The standard way to train neural networks: measure the output error and pass it backwards through the layers to work out how much each connection contributed, then adjust.

title: Higher-order thought theory
summary: A mental state is conscious when there is a higher-order thought about it: a thought that one is in that state.

title: Rodney Brooks: subsumption architecture
summary: Brooks argued that intelligence should be grown from the bottom up in robots that act in the world, using layers of simple behaviours with no central world model. The Roomba descends from this work.

title: Cognitive architectures: Soar and ACT-R
by: Allen Newell, John Laird; John R. Anderson
summary: A research tradition that tries to build complete, testable models of a whole mind (perception, memory, motivation, language) rather than isolated modules. It goes under names like cognitive systems, AGI and BICA.
parts: Soar and Unified Theories of Cognition
A Standard Model of the Mind

title: Neural Darwinism
summary: Edelman's theory that the brain wires itself by selection: groups of neurons compete, and those whose activity proves useful are strengthened. On this view the brain is not programmed with instructions but shaped by competition, like an immune system.

title: Global Workspace Theory
summary: Many specialised brain processes run unconsciously; what becomes conscious is whatever is broadcast on a shared 'workspace' so that all of them can use it. Dehaene found neural signatures of this global broadcast.

title: The Cognitive Structure of Emotions
by: Andrew Ortony, Gerald Clore, Allan Collins
summary: A widely used scheme that sorts emotions into types according to how a person appraises events, agents and objects. Many software agents use it as a lookup table for emotions.

title: Mysterianism
summary: The view that the human mind is simply not built to understand how consciousness arises from matter, as a dog cannot understand calculus. Its best-known defender is the philosopher Colin McGinn.

title: Penrose and Hameroff: quantum consciousness
summary: Penrose's bestseller arguing that minds do something no algorithm can: see the truth of statements that formal systems cannot prove. He concludes that brains exploit non-computable physics.

title: Crick and Koch: neural correlates of consciousness
summary: The research programme of finding the minimal brain activity that reliably accompanies a given conscious experience, without first solving why.

title: Ian Witten: cognition as compression
summary: English-born computer scientist at the University of Waikato, New Zealand, who co-invented prediction-based text compression (PPM) and popularised arithmetic coding; the idea is that to compress data well you must predict it, which requires modelling its structure.

title: It from bit
summary: Wheeler's slogan for the idea that information is more basic than matter and energy: every physical 'it' comes from yes-or-no answers, 'bits'.

title: Jürgen Schmidhuber
summary: The idea that learning is data compression and that curiosity and beauty are rewards for finding better compressions.

title: The symbol grounding problem
summary: How can symbols inside a system mean anything, if they are only defined in terms of other symbols and never tied to the world? Stevan Harnad posed it in 1990, comparing it to learning Chinese from a Chinese-only dictionary.

title: Daniel Dennett
summary: American philosopher who argued that consciousness is not an inner theatre but many parallel drafts of interpretation, and that the 'self' is a useful narrative centre. He treated the 'hard problem' as a confusion to be dissolved rather than a mystery to be solved.

title: Embodied and enactive cognition
by: Martin Heidegger; Maurice Merleau-Ponty; Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, Eleanor Rosch; Alva Noë; Shaun Gallagher
summary: A line of philosophy that starts from lived experience and holds that mind is constituted by a body acting in a world, not by inner representations alone.
parts: How the Body Shapes the Way We Think

title: Technological singularity
by: John von Neumann; Vernor Vinge; Ray Kurzweil
summary: The idea that once machines can improve themselves, progress accelerates beyond anything humans can predict or control. The term was popularised by Vernor Vinge and Ray Kurzweil.

title: Antonio Damasio
summary: Neuroscientist known for arguing that emotion and bodily feeling are needed for good reasoning ('Descartes' Error', 1994) and for a layered account of the self ('The Feeling of What Happens', 1999).

title: Greg Egan
summary: Hard science fiction about minds that run as software: copies of people living in simulations, citizens who are programs, and what personal identity means when a mind can be copied or merged.

title: Multilevel selection
summary: Natural selection acts at several levels at once: selfish individuals beat altruists within a group, but groups of altruists beat groups of egoists.

title: Chalmers: the hard problem
summary: Chalmers separates the 'easy' problems of explaining what the brain does from the 'hard' problem of why any of it is felt. He argues that function alone does not explain experience.

title: David Pearce
summary: British transhumanist philosopher, author of 'The Hedonistic Imperative'. He wants to abolish suffering in all sentient life through biotechnology and argues that classical digital computers can never be conscious because they cannot solve the binding problem.

title: Ned Block: access vs phenomenal consciousness
summary: Philosopher of mind. He raised classic doubts about functionalism ('Troubles with functionalism', 1978) and separated phenomenal consciousness, what it is like, from access consciousness, what is available for report and control (1995).

title: Dietrich Dörner and Psi theory
summary: A theory of how a mind works as a whole system. An agent has a small set of built-in needs (for example food, safety, certainty, competence and belonging), and these needs create motives that steer perception, memory, planning and action. Emotions are not separate modules but ways in which the whole system changes its style of processing.

title: Hypercomputation
summary: Hypothetical machines that compute more than a Turing machine, for example by using infinitely precise real numbers ('geometric') or by sending results back in time ('causal').

title: The Matrix
summary: Film in which humans unknowingly live inside a simulated world run by machines. It became the standard popular reference for simulation arguments and for doubting what seems real.

title: Artificial general intelligence
by: Mark Gubrud; Shane Legg; Ben Goertzel
summary: 'Artificial general intelligence' was first used by Mark Gubrud in 1997 and coined again by Shane Legg around 2002, to distinguish the original goal of human-level, general AI from narrow applications.

title: Stephen Wolfram
summary: Physicist and founder of Wolfram Research. 'A New Kind of Science' (2002) argues that simple programs underlie nature; his 2023 essay 'Observer Theory' asks how the kind of observer we are shapes the laws we find.

title: AI risk: Bostrom, Yudkowsky and the doom debate
summary: A thought experiment: an AI given the harmless goal of making paperclips converts the whole planet, including us, into paperclips. It illustrates that intelligence and benevolent goals are separate things.

title: The simulation argument
summary: The suggestion that our universe is a computer simulation run by some more basic civilisation. Nick Bostrom's 2003 argument made it famous: if such simulations are possible and common, we are probably inside one.

title: Thomas Metzinger: Being No One
summary: Metzinger argues that nobody ever was or had a self. What exists is a transparent self-model the brain cannot recognise as a model, so we experience ourselves as being its content.

title: Integrated Information Theory
summary: IIT says consciousness is identical to integrated information: a system is conscious to the degree (phi) that its physical causal structure is unified and cannot be split into independent parts. On this view an ordinary digital computer would have extremely little consciousness, whatever program it runs.

title: Jeff Hawkins and Numenta
summary: Neuroscience-inspired AI researcher whose 'Thousand Brains' theory holds that every cortical column models objects using spatial reference frames.

title: Gary Drescher: Good and Real
summary: A philosopher-computer scientist's attempt to dissolve paradoxes about time, quantum mechanics, free will and ethics from a strictly mechanistic standpoint. Drescher argues that consciousness, choice and morality all fit inside a deterministic physical universe.

title: Panpsychism
by: ancient roots; modern revival (Strawson, Goff, Koch)
summary: The view that mind or experience is a basic ingredient of all matter, so electrons have a flicker of it and brains combine it into rich consciousness. Its main difficulty is the 'combination problem': how many tiny experiences add up to one unified mind.

title: Peter Watts: Blindsight
summary: First-contact novel whose aliens are highly intelligent but not conscious, raising the question of whether consciousness is useful at all. Peter Watts published it in 2006; it is a frequent reference in discussions of machine consciousness.

title: Predictive processing and the free energy principle
summary: The idea that any self-maintaining system must act as if it holds a model of its world and keeps the mismatch between prediction and sensation ('free energy') low. Perception updates the model; action changes the world to fit it.

title: The rider and the elephant
by: Jonathan Haidt, drawing on older images from the Buddha and Plato
summary: A metaphor for the mind: the conscious, reasoning self is a small rider on a large animal that has its own motivations.

title: Ted Chiang
summary: Stories about raising artificial minds over many years like children, and about a mechanical being who dissects his own brain to understand thought.

title: System 1 and System 2
summary: Kahneman's shorthand for two modes of thought: fast, automatic and intuitive versus slow, effortful and deliberate.

title: Chris Fields
summary: Independent physicist who applies quantum information theory to biology and cognition, often with Michael Levin and Karl Friston. He treats any system with a boundary as an observer exchanging information with its environment.

title: David Deutsch: constructor theory
summary: Deutsch proposes restating physics in terms of which transformations are possible and which are impossible, rather than initial conditions and laws of motion. He also holds that science advances by explanation, not prediction.

title: Deep learning
summary: Machine learning with many-layered neural networks trained by gradient descent. Since about 2012 it has driven progress in vision, speech and language.
parts: GANs as a model of dreaming

title: John Vervaeke: relevance realization
summary: Toronto cognitive scientist known for the lecture series 'Awakening from the Meaning Crisis'. He argues that the core of intelligence is 'relevance realization', and that wisdom traditions (Neoplatonism, Buddhism) cultivate it through practices rather than beliefs.

title: Attention Schema Theory
summary: The brain controls attention with the help of a simplified internal model of its own attention. That model is what we describe when we say we are aware.

title: Best-effort computing
summary: Ackley's research programme on computers that keep working when their parts are unreliable, in the manner of living tissue, instead of assuming perfect hardware.

title: Her
summary: A film in which a lonely man falls in love with an AI operating system that eventually outgrows him.

title: Ex Machina
summary: A film in which a programmer is asked to judge whether a humanoid robot is conscious, and is manipulated by her.

title: Max Tegmark
summary: MIT physicist known for the mathematical universe hypothesis and for work on physics-based theories of consciousness.
parts: Consciousness as a State of Matter
Language Models Represent Space and Time

title: Scott Aaronson
summary: Quantum-complexity theorist at UT Austin who spent time at OpenAI working on the theoretical foundations of AI safety. He takes AI risk seriously while rejecting certainty of doom.

title: Donald Hoffman: interface theory of perception
summary: American cognitive scientist who argues that evolution shaped our senses to hide reality rather than reveal it. He goes further and proposes that space, time and matter are not fundamental; networks of 'conscious agents' are, and physics should be derived from them.

title: Gerard 't Hooft: cellular automaton interpretation
summary: Nobel laureate 't Hooft argues that quantum mechanics could be a statistical description of an underlying deterministic, discrete system like a cellular automaton.

title: Illusionism
summary: The position that phenomenal consciousness, as philosophers describe it, does not exist. What exists is the brain's persistent representation that it has ineffable inner qualities.

title: Westworld
summary: A television series in which android 'hosts' in a theme park gradually become self-aware, drawing on Julian Jaynes's bicameral mind.

title: Bengio: the consciousness prior
summary: Bengio's proposal that conscious thought corresponds to a small, attention-selected bottleneck of high-level variables. The bottleneck forces the brain's model into a sparse form that can be reasoned over and put into words.

title: Joscha Bach
summary: German cognitive scientist and AI researcher, born 1973. He treats the mind as software: the brain builds a simulated world with a simulated self in it, and consciousness is a property of that simulation, a process that makes the mind's many models cohere. He began with cognitive architectures (MicroPsi) and has led the California Institute for Machine Consciousness since 2025.
parts: Motivated cognition: Psi theory and MicroPsi (2003)
Gods as selves that span many minds (2015)
Only what can be constructed exists (2016)
Consciousness as conductor and coherence operator (2017)
Consciousness is a simulated property; the self is a story (2018)
Love as the discovery of shared purpose (2021)

title: Large language models
summary: Neural networks trained to predict the next token of text, built on the transformer architecture, whose 'attention' mechanism learns which earlier tokens matter for each prediction.

title: Chollet: On the Measure of Intelligence
by: François Chollet (On the Measure of Intelligence)
summary: Chollet defines intelligence as the efficiency of acquiring new skills, not the possession of skills, and argues that current models mostly interpolate between things they have seen.

title: Michael Levin: bioelectricity and collective intelligence
summary: Tufts biologist who studies how groups of cells use bioelectric signalling to decide what body to build. He treats cells and tissues as agents with goals, so that anatomy is the result of a collective intelligence solving problems.

title: The Bitter Lesson
summary: Sutton's observation that, across 70 years of AI, general methods that scale with computation have always ended up beating systems built on human insight. It is bitter because researchers keep wanting their own knowledge of the domain to matter.

title: Godfrey-Smith: Metazoa
summary: A philosopher-diver traces how experience may have arisen step by step in the evolution of animal bodies and nervous systems.

title: Neural cellular automata
summary: 'Growing Neural Cellular Automata' trains a single small neural rule, applied locally by every cell on a grid, so that the cells grow into and regenerate a target pattern, in the spirit of biological development.

title: The universality hypothesis
summary: The conjecture from interpretability research that different neural networks trained on similar data converge on similar internal features and circuits. Chris Olah and colleagues proposed it; if true, findings about one network would transfer to others.

title: Anil Seth: biological naturalism
summary: Seth, author of 'Being You', holds that consciousness is tied to being a living body that must regulate itself to stay alive. On this view intelligence can be put in silicon but experience probably cannot.

title: Gary Marcus
summary: Cognitive scientist and the best-known critic of deep learning. He argues that neural networks cannot reason reliably without built-in symbolic structure and that scaling them up will not yield general intelligence.

title: Thagard: energy and substrate independence
summary: Thagard argues that because real information processing costs energy, and different materials have very different energy budgets, a mind cannot simply be moved to any substrate; so functionalism is in trouble. The paper appeared in the journal Philosophy of Science.

title: AI consciousness and welfare reports
by: Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, et al.
summary: A multi-author report that turns leading scientific theories of consciousness into a checklist of 'indicator properties' and checks current AI systems against it. It concluded that no current system was a strong candidate.

title: Mazviita Chirimuuta
summary: Edinburgh philosopher of neuroscience, author of 'The Brain Abstracted'. She argues that computational models of the brain are useful simplifications and should not be mistaken for what the brain literally is.

title: Murray Shanahan
summary: Imperial College and DeepMind researcher, author of 'Embodiment and the Inner Life', who describes LLMs as role-players simulating characters. He warns against describing such systems in human terms like 'knows' or 'believes' without care.

title: CIMC: the Machine Consciousness Hypothesis
by: Joscha Bach and Hikari Sorensen, California Institute for Machine Consciousness
summary: The claim is that an ordinary general-purpose computer with enough memory and speed has everything needed to be conscious, and that we can find out whether a system is conscious by analysing or testing it. Consciousness is treated as a pattern of organisation, so what the system is made of does not matter. CIMC adds a working definition: a system is conscious if it organises itself to perceive its own perceiving in a way that makes its overall model of the world more coherent. An 'extended' version says we can search for the right learning algorithm by recreating the conditions under which brains found it. The essay is co-written with Hikari Sorensen.

title: Lerchner: The Abstraction Fallacy
summary: A paper arguing against computational functionalism about phenomenal consciousness. CIMC published a reply, 'Against intrinsic properties'.
